summary: This informational document sets out a framework for traceability in the Interface to the Routing System (I2RS). It explains the motivation, requirements and use cases, and defines an information model for recording interactions between I2RS components. The goal is a consistent way to log what was done, by which component, and when, which helps with operating and debugging the system.

eli5.summary: Imagine a school office where every change to the class schedule gets written in a logbook: who changed it, what they changed, and when. This is a plan for keeping that kind of logbook for the machines that control network routes.

subtitle: Recording what clients ask the routing system to do

tldr.problem: The I2RS (Interface to the Routing System) allows external clients to make routing changes, but operators need to understand what was changed, by whom, and when for troubleshooting, auditing, and forensics.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a standard information model for I2RS trace logs that records client identity, timestamps, requested and applied operations, operation data, result codes, and state transitions, creating an auditable record of all routing changes.
tldr.outcome: Operators can trace routing changes back to their requesting client, understand what was attempted versus what succeeded, and correlate changes with network events for troubleshooting and compliance.

facts.label: Trace log retrieval methods
facts.value: Syslog (optional), I2RS Information Collection (optional), I2RS Pub/Sub (mandatory)

today: RFC 7922 is an Informational RFC published in June 2016 as part of the I2RS working group deliverables. It has not been obsoleted. The information model it defines remains the baseline for I2RS traceability and continues to guide implementations and operational procedures for organizations deploying I2RS in their networks.

sections.title: I2RS and the Need for Traceability
sections.content: The Interface to the Routing System (I2RS) is a protocol that allows external clients to query and modify routing state on network devices. Unlike traditional router configuration, I2RS allows high-throughput, real-time, fine-grained changes to routing decisions. I2RS clients must authenticate to an I2RS agent on a routing device and provide unique identities. When many I2RS clients make changes concurrently or in rapid succession, network operators need visibility into which changes were made, which client requested them, what the result was, and when they occurred. This document defines the standard framework and information model for recording these interactions in a trace log.
sections.eli5: Many remote controllers can now adjust how network traffic flows. To debug problems, you need to know who changed what and when.

sections.title: Why Traceability Matters
sections.content: As networks scale and policy becomes more sophisticated, operational complexity increases. I2RS offers granular control but removes the locality of policy that would typically be configured on individual devices. A single change from an I2RS client might trigger routing updates across many devices. Multiple changes occurring concurrently or in sequence could cause race conditions, performance issues, data loss, or service disruption. Operators need event-level granularity in tracing to identify the sequence of changes that led to a problem. Additionally, many organizations have audit and compliance requirements to log configuration and runtime changes, and I2RS trace logs provide the standardized structure needed for automated tools, anomaly detection, and forensic analysis.
sections.eli5: When one change causes a cascade of others and something breaks, you need to see the chain of events to find the culprit.

sections.title: I2RS Trace Log Information Model
sections.content: Each I2RS trace log entry records the lifecycle of a single I2RS operation. Key fields include: Event ID (unique identifier, can be reused across state transitions for a single operation), Starting and Ending Timestamps (in RFC 3339 format with fractional seconds for microsecond granularity), Request State (PENDING, IN PROCESS, or COMPLETED), Client Identity (the authenticated I2RS client), Client Priority (from access control), Secondary Identity (an opaque identifier from a controlling application), Client Address (network address of the client), Requested Operation and Applied Operation (which may differ if the request was modified), Requested and Applied Operation Data, Transaction ID (for grouping related operations), Result Code, and Timeout Occurred (boolean). An End Of Message marker distinguishes one record from the next.
sections.eli5: Each log entry is like a receipt: it shows who asked for what, when it happened, what state it was in, and whether it worked.

sections.title: Log Creation and Storage
sections.content: The I2RS agent creates and maintains the trace log as it processes client operations. Logs can be stored in memory buffers for recent operations or as files on the agent's local storage. Since I2RS operations may not complete synchronously or within bounded time, buffering may be required to ensure fields like Operation and Result Code are captured in the same record. Organizations should implement trace log rotation to prevent resource exhaustion, supporting rotation based on time or file size with multiple archived logs. The duration for retaining log data should consider data protection policies: the longer logs are retained, the higher the risk if they are leaked. Organizations may need to anonymize sensitive attributes in logs for privacy compliance.
sections.eli5: Write changes to a logbook; keep it from getting too full by archiving old entries; protect it because it contains sensitive information.

sections.title: Log Example and Retrieval Methods
sections.content: A trace log entry might record: Event ID 1, timestamp 2013-09-03T12:00:01.21+00:00, state COMPLETED, I2RS client 5CEF1870-0326-11E2-A21F-0800200C9A66, priority 100, secondary ID com.example.RoutingApp, client address 2001:db8:c0c0::2, requested operation ROUTE_ADD, applied operation ROUTE_ADD (same), operation data showing a route prefix 2001:db8:feed:: with prefix length 64 and next-hop 2001:db8:cafe::1, transaction ID 2763461, result code SUCCESS(0), ending timestamp 2013-09-03T12:00:01.23+00:00. Trace logs can be retrieved via three methods: Syslog (RFC 5424) with structured data elements for machine parsing, I2RS Information Collection via snapshot or subscription stream, or I2RS Pub/Sub (mandatory to implement) for a live stream of interactions that subscribers can log, aggregate, and analyze flexibly.
sections.eli5: The log shows what changed, which client made the request, when, and if it worked. You can pull the log through different systems for different uses.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Safeguards
sections.content: I2RS trace logs are sensitive: they reveal router state, identifying information about clients and their interactions, and may contain security-sensitive attributes. The RFC does not specify how to protect stored logs, but it recommends security best practices: disk encryption, restrictive file permissions, hardening and physical security of logging entities, mutual authentication, transport encryption for log transfers, channel confidentiality and integrity protection. Operators should anonymize or obfuscate sensitive information in logs to ensure privacy. The security model depends on the organization's own policies and regulatory requirements, as the RFC correctly notes that this is outside its scope.
sections.eli5: These logs contain secrets: protect them with encryption, limited access, and secure storage.
